prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clear invention in the sense of the 'discovery or invention' criterion: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the lattice light shift, and the first strontium demonstration showed that many atoms can be interrogated without trap-induced perturbation. Ye's group then carried the concept to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and to many-body-aware clock operation. The result is independently reproduced in many laboratories, is already used in international clock comparisons, and underpins tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the prospective redefinition of the second. This is also the candidate with by far the broadest opening support: six of eight members placed it in their top three and all eight ranked it, three of them first. The two-name credit is compact and defensible, and Hall and Hänsch were honoured in 2005 for comb technology, so this is not a repeat of an earlier prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are about attribution and about how far the prize would reach. Lattice-clock work involved other groups (for example Lemonde and Gill on neutral-atom and ion clocks, and Hinkley, Ludlow and others in Ye's own group and at NIST/JILA), and a two-name prize necessarily simplifies that history. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so a critic could say that the full practical payoff is still pending. There is also a risk that the committee rewards precision metrology that was already partly recognised through the 2005 comb prize, rather than a distinctly new principle. I take these as qualifications rather than disqualifications, because the magic-wavelength idea is separable and original.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first on the strength of Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium demonstration, with Ye bringing the implementation to the 1e-18 level, and places atom interferometry (B001) second.
responses.response: I agree that the Katori-Ye split is the cleanest attribution on the table, and I share the view that the invention is original. Where I part from Kroll is on B001. Atom interferometry has a more tangled credit story (Pritchard, Bordé, Kasevich and also Chu, whose name is not in the credited triple), and only three members ranked it at all, so I do not think it is ready as a prize configuration. I would keep it out of my alternatives for that reason, while acknowledging that its scientific importance for inertial sensing is real.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery (B052) first as a clear observational discovery that opened a new window on the universe, while conceding that a three-person split simplifies a very large collaboration with AMANDA precursors.
responses.response: I take the point that B052 is a discovery of nature in the strictest sense, and the committee should not undervalue it simply because optical clocks are an invention. My serious qualification is attribution. Danielsson himself notes that the collaboration is large and that precursor contributors are left out; Pearce's own opening drops Spiering and credits only Halzen and Karle, which shows that the names are not settled even among supporters. With only three members ranking B052 at all and just two placing it in the top three, I do not see the support or the clean credit that would justify preferring it now. I would be willing to look again if the committee can agree who the people responsible are.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first and optical lattice clocks second, arguing that neutrino astronomy became a working discipline through the diffuse flux and later blazar association.
responses.response: I agree with Pearce that B052 and B009 are the two strongest scientific stories, and the difference between us is mainly on maturity of attribution. Pearce's assessment of Katori and Ye matches mine, which is reassuring because he sees the same clean division between the concept and the precision frontier. Where I would press is on his own two-name IceCube credit: if the committee takes Pearce's view, it must justify excluding Spiering, and that debate is not yet resolved in the record. On balance, I would rather settle a prize where both names are uncontested.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B008) first and Cirac-Zoller (B014) second, valuing circuit QED as the architecture for on-chip quantum optics and the Cirac-Zoller proposals as the first blueprint for scalable quantum computation.
responses.response: I respect the importance of both, but I do not think circuit QED is as ready as the clocks. B008 received only one first-place ranking and was ranked by four members, and its credited triple (Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf) omits other contributors to the 2004 proposal and to the experimental realisation, which will be contested. For Cirac-Zoller I agree the pair is clean, but the prize would then be for theory proposals whose experimental realisations belong to others, including Wineland, who was honoured in 2012. I would keep it on the table as a strong later candidate, not as the configuration for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the unrealized redefinition of the second as a reason to wait for a metrological milestone.
Whether contributions by other lattice-clock groups would be judged substantial enough to complicate a two-name credit.
Whether IceCube (B052) could reach a settled three-person attribution by the next round, which could change the relative ranking.
How much weight the committee should give to instrument invention versus discovery, which matters for my alternative B017.
statement.conflict_note: I ranked B017 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) first in my opening ballot. It lies in my own field of transmission electron microscopy, and and given my leadership role in the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy (reported as president in 2024) I could be seen as having a professional stake. I therefore treat my support for B017 with caution, list it only as a secondary alternative, and would accept recusal from any decision concerning it. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, so I flag this for transparency, but no specific conflict is apparent regarding B009, B018, B052 or the other candidates from the provided profile.
